propositions.text: The principal and associate Appellants, citizens of Nepal, appeal the RPD decision rejecting their refugee claims.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXXthe associate Appellant), citizens of Nepal, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated September 7, 2017, rejecting their claim(s) for refugee protection.

propositions.text: Appellants submit new evidence with the appeal under subsection 110(4) IRPA and request an oral hearing under subsection 110(6).
propositions.quote: The Appellants have submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),1 and request an oral hearing be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants, Nepalese citizens, appeal the RPD's rejection and submit new evidence requesting an oral hearing under IRPA provisions.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's rejection of refugee protection claims under IRPA.

propositions.text: Appellants allege fear of persecution and harm by Maoists due to non-support and principal Appellant's NCP support.
propositions.quote: They allege that they fear persecution and fear that Maoists will abduct, physically harm, or kill them because of a failure to support them or comply with their demands, as well as the principal Appellant's long time support of the Nepali Congress Party (NCP).

propositions.text: Maoists began demanding donations in 2001, escalating to three abductions with death threats; last abduction in September 2015.
propositions.quote: They allege that Maoists began demanding "donations" in 2001. The demands escalated and resulted in three abductions where death threats were made should they not comply with the increasing demands for money. The last abduction took place in September 2015.

propositions.text: Appellants fled Nepal in 2015 after last abduction.
propositions.quote: The Appellants fled Nepal in XXXX 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants allege Maoist persecution including abductions and threats since 2001, fleeing Nepal in 2015.

propositions.text: RPD hearing held August 24, 2017; RPD rejected claim on September 7, 2017, finding viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' hearing for refugee protection was held on August 24, 2017. In a decision on September 7, 2017, the RPD rejected the Appellants' claim finding that they had a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kathmandu, Nepal.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred in IFA assessment because Maoists have nationwide network.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFA location because the Maoists have a nationwide network.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claim citing IFA in Kathmandu; Appellants argue this was erroneous due to Maoists' nationwide reach.

propositions.text: RAD applies correctness standard for fact and mixed fact-law questions per Huruglica.
propositions.quote: For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, the RAD has applied the standard of correctness as per Huruglica.

propositions.text: RAD applies modified reasonableness standard for credibility issues where RPD has meaningful advantage per X (Re).
propositions.quote: In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, I may apply the RAD modified standard of reasonableness in those situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage as per the decision in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies correctness standard for fact and mixed questions, and modified reasonableness for credibility where RPD has advantage.

propositions.text: Appellants submitted personal affidavit and Maoist Threat Letter with courier envelope as new evidence.
propositions.quote: In support of this appeal, the Appellants submitted a personal affidavit and a Maoist Threat Letter, along with the courier envelope,2 as proposed new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants submitted a personal affidavit and Maoist Threat Letter as new evidence on appeal.

propositions.text: Subsection 110(4) IRPA limits new evidence to that arising after rejection or not reasonably available before.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected3 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

propositions.text: Appellants must make detailed submissions on how new evidence meets subsection 110(4) and relates to them.
propositions.quote: It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.4

paragraphs.summary: The court explains subsection 110(4) IRPA limits new evidence and requires detailed submissions on its relevance and timing.

propositions.text: If new evidence meets subsection 110(4), RAD applies adapted Raza factors from Singh for credibility, relevance, newness.
propositions.quote: In addition, if the new evidence meets one of the explicit legislative factors in subsection 110(4), then the second step of the analysis is for the RAD to apply the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.

propositions.text: Singh holds RAD assesses new evidence admissibility for credibility, relevance, newness; excludes Raza's materiality factor.
propositions.quote: In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD is not to consider the fourth Raza factor of materiality to the admission of new evidence, which is a consideration for subsection 110(6) and the request for an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies adapted Raza factors per Singh to assess new evidence admissibility for credibility, relevance, and newness.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant's affidavit arose after claim rejection and meets subsection 110(4) requirements; will be assessed under adapted Raza factors.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the affidavit arose after the rejection of the Appellants' claim and meets the basic requirements of subsection 110(4); it will be assessed applying the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.

propositions.text: Affidavit states principal Appellant's brother in Kathmandu was threatened by Maoists seeking the Appellants, told not to go to police.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that it provides a statement indicating that his brother who lives in Kathmandu called him and stated that three Maoists came to his home and gave him a letter indicating that they are looking for the principal Appellant and his wife. The Maoists threatened his brother, telling him not to go to the police.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the affidavit arose after rejection, meets subsection 110(4), and recounts Maoists threatening the Appellant's brother in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Maoist Threat Letter dated October 2, 2017 arose after claim rejection, meets subsection 110(4); will be assessed under adapted Raza factors.
propositions.quote: As well, the RAD has reviewed the Maoist Threat Letter dated October 2, 2017, which indicates it arose following the rejection of the Appellants' claim, meeting the basic requirements of subsection 110(4). The RAD must further assess the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh, where the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness.

propositions.text: Appellants' Maoist problems occurred at home with a separatist Maoist splinter group called the Biplav faction.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes on its review of the evidence in the record that all of the Appellants' problems with the Maoists occurred in their home and are with a separatist Maoist faction (a splinter group) described as the Biplav faction (Netra Bikram Chand Biplav).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Maoist Threat Letter arose after rejection and notes Appellants' Maoist issues involve the Biplav splinter faction.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows Maoist faction splits: Baidya split from UCPN-M in 2012 forming Maoist NCP-M; Biplav faction formed in 2014 from Baidya faction.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence states that a faction of Maoists led by Mohan Baidya [Vaidya] split from the UCPN-M in 2012 to create the Maoist NCP-M. Baidya was described as a "communist hard-liner" leading a "dissenting faction of the ruling Maoist party." Nekram Bikram Chandra was the Secretary of this faction, which became known as the CPN-M. A further split in the Baidya faction in 2014 led to the formation of the Biplav or Biplab faction of the CPN-M, which became known as the CPN-Biplav or Chand faction.

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence details Maoist faction splits, including the 2014 formation of the Biplav faction from Baidya's group.

propositions.text: The Biplav faction consists of former combatants rejecting government accommodation and engages in criminal activity and extortion.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the documentary evidence indicates that this group, composed of former, frustrated combatants and other factions that have rejected accommodation with the elected government, is involved in criminal activity and extortion.

paragraphs.summary: The Biplav faction is composed of former combatants rejecting government and involved in criminal activity and extortion.

propositions.text: The Maoist Threat Letter lacks identifying info, has simple letterhead, hand-filled with minimal security, signed by 'In Charge'.
propositions.quote: The letter indicates that it is issued by the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist), Area 3, but it does not provide any further information to identify where it arose from or whether there is any association with the Biplav group that the Appellants allege are the agents of persecution. The letterhead is of simple design and could be produced by any individual with basic word-processing skills and a printer. The letter is hand-filled, with no security features beyond a signature from someone who describes themselves as "In Charge."

paragraphs.summary: The Maoist Threat Letter is unsigned with minimal security and lacks clear association with the Biplav faction.

propositions.text: Since 2006, CPN-M, UCPN, and YCL stopped issuing threat letters due to democratic participation and monitoring.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the documentary evidence indicates that since the 2006 Comprehensive Peace Agreement, "CPN-M, UCPN [and] YCL have stopped issuing threat letters," because they have been part of the democratic process and government since then, and because human rights groups and the media monitor political parties and their activities, including the Maoists, which makes sending threat letters "a political blunder."

propositions.text: Threat letters were widespread 1996-2006, few during 2006-2009, none documented after 2010 by Maoist groups.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence carries on to note that there are no cases of the issuance of threat letters currently by the CPN-M, UCPN, and YCL. Threat letters were a "widespread" practice during the conflict between 1996 and 2006, and then a "few" were issued during the peace process between 2006 and 2009. After 2009, INSEC has documented "some cases of oral threats and beatings," but is not aware of cases of threat letters issued by Maoist groups since 2010." Another NGO, the AHRC, stated that the UCPN, CPN-M and YCL did issue threat letters before 2006, but was not aware of any cases of such threat letters being issued after these parties joined "mainstream politics."

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence shows Maoist groups ceased issuing threat letters after 2006 due to political participation and monitoring.

propositions.text: Letters like the submitted threat letter are not used currently and have not been seen by agencies for some time.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the documentary evidence indicates that letters such as that submitted as new evidence are not utilized in the current environment in Nepal, and that they have not been seen by any of the agencies referred to in the evidence for some time.

propositions.text: AHRC reports many forgery cases of threat letters; letterheads and stamps can be cheaply and easily produced in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence further states that the AHRC has come across "a lot of forgery cases" where people have obtained letters speaking about "threats and demands." The AHRC representative also noted that in Nepal, one can "easily" design a letterhead and a stamp for less than US$5 at any "designing outlet."

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds such threat letters are not currently used and are often forged, with cheap letterheads easily produced in Nepal.

propositions.text: Prevalence of fraudulent documents does not mean every threat letter is false, but this document must be considered with caution.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes that the prevalence of fraudulent documents does not mean that every single "Threat Letter" document is necessarily false. However, the RAD finds in the context of all of the concerns noted above, that it must consider this document with caution.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD cautions that while many threat letters are fraudulent, each must be carefully considered, including this one.

propositions.text: Last Maoist event involving Appellants was September 2015; RPD noted no Maoist action for extended period and family in Kathmandu had no problems.
propositions.quote: The RPD issued its decision in September 2017, clearly stating that there had been no action by the Maoists for an extended period of time, noting that the principal Appellant's brother and the Appellants' son lived in Kathmandu without any interaction or problems from Maoists.

propositions.text: It is unusual Maoists took no action for two years, then suddenly threatened Appellant's brother after RPD decision.
propositions.quote: It seems unusual that there would be no response or actions by the Maoists to seek out the Appellants or their family members for two years, and then shortly following the RPD decision, the Maoists appear at the Appellant's brother's home in Kathmandu and leave a letter threatening the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no Maoist action for two years; the RAD finds it unusual Maoists suddenly threatened the Appellant's brother after the RPD decision.

propositions.text: The coincidence of Maoists reappearing days after negative decision is suspicious and reduces credibility of affidavit.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that it is too much of a coincidence that mere days after the issuance of a negative decision in this claim, the Maoists suddenly reappeared seeking the Appellants.

propositions.text: Federal Court in Ankrah held that a series of chance events can justify disbelief of testimony as too fortuitous.
propositions.quote: With regard to this coincidence, the RAD is guided by the Federal Court decision in Ankrah, where J. Noel stated: The applicant's story does otherwise reveal a series of events of chance, and it was open to the tribunal to conclude therefrom that the Applicant's testimony was too fortuitous in nature to be believed.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the timing suspicious and cites Ankrah to support disbelief of fortuitous testimony.

propositions.text: Meng decision held suspicious timing of events can justify skepticism of claim credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD has additionally considered the decision in Meng where the Court held that: ...the Board's remark that the timing of the alleged church raid is an "extraordinary coincidence" that is suspiciously convenient is not unreasonable in light of the evidence...

paragraphs.summary: The RAD cites Meng to support that suspicious timing of events can justify skepticism of credibility.

propositions.text: The timing coincidence is improbable and likely fabricated to bolster appeal; affidavit is not credible on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that is not unreasonable to infer that the coincidence of the timing of the events is improbable and that the renewed actions by the Maoists was not a coincidence, but a carefully concocted addition to enhance the appeal and to bolster the authenticity of the story. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that this coincidence is a reasonable cause to assign little probative value to the events described in the principal Appellant's affidavit and finds it is not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the timing coincidence improbable and the affidavit not credible, likely fabricated to bolster the appeal.

propositions.text: The RAD finds evidentiary basis to undermine the credibility of the Appellants' 'Threat Letter' and assigns it no evidentiary weight.
propositions.quote: The RAD further finds that upon a review of all of the findings in respect to the Appellants' "Threat Letter," there is an evidentiary basis to undermine its credibility and assign no evidentiary weight to the document.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the 'Threat Letter' lacks credibility and assigns it no evidentiary weight.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the new evidence does not meet credibility requirements of adapted Raza factors and will not be admitted.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the new evidence does not meet the credibility requirements of the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh16 and the documents will not be admitted as new evidence in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds new evidence fails credibility requirements and refuses to admit it.

propositions.text: The RAD may hold a hearing if documentary evidence raises a serious credibility issue central to the refugee claim and justifies allowing or rejecting it.
propositions.quote: The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD may hold a hearing if documentary evidence raises serious credibility issues central to the refugee claim.

propositions.text: The RAD denies the application for an oral hearing as no admissible new evidence was submitted.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have submitted no admissible new evidence in support of their appeal. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the RPD's record; the application for an oral hearing is denied.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD denies the oral hearing application due to lack of admissible new evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD found the determinative issue is the availability of an IFA in Kathmandu, Nepal.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the determinative issue is the availability of an IFA in Kathmandu, Nepal.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue Kathmandu is far from their home area where they had problems with Maoists.
propositions.quote: Kathmandu is XXXX XXXX from the Appellants' home area where they have encountered their past problems with the Maoists.

propositions.text: The Maoists have a nationwide network and operate throughout Nepal.
propositions.quote: The Maoists have a nationwide network and operate throughout the country.

propositions.text: The Maoists are the ruling party and effectively state actors, so Appellants have no IFA anywhere in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The Maoists are currently the ruling party in Nepal, and that the agents of persecution in this case are, therefore, effectively state actors. Given that the Maoists hold power at the highest level of the Nepali government, and the government is ubiquitous in Nepal, it defies reason to suggest that the Appellants have an IFA anywhere in the country.

propositions.text: Maoists have visited the principal Appellant's parents multiple times, showing intent to find and kill the Appellants.
propositions.quote: The Maoists have continued to visit the principal Appellant's parents inXXXX XXXX (they have returned on 3-4 occasions since the Appellants left Nepal) and insist that they are intent on finding and killing the Appellants, demonstrating the extent to which the agents of persecution have maintained their desire and resolve to locate and harm the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the key issue is IFA availability; the Appellants argue Maoists' nationwide power and intent negate any IFA in Nepal.

propositions.text: The RAD must apply the two-pronged Rasaratnam test to assess an IFA's viability.
propositions.quote: In assessing an IFA, the RAD must apply a two-pronged test cited in the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Rasaratnam:18 1) the Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. 2) moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD must apply the two-pronged Rasaratnam test to assess IFA viability.

propositions.text: Both prongs of the Rasaratnam test must be satisfied to find an IFA; burden rests on Appellants to show no IFA.
propositions.quote: Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellants have an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose taking into account the Appellants' identities. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The Appellants cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.19

paragraphs.summary: Both Rasaratnam prongs must be met to find an IFA; Appellants bear burden to disprove IFA existence.

propositions.text: Canadian courts hold large urban areas cannot be assumed IFAs by population size alone; distance from persecutors is not determinative.
propositions.quote: While an analysis of whether a particular appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA under the first prong of the Rasaratnam test is necessarily fact-specific, the RAD is aware that as a general principle, Canadian courts have held that large urban areas cannot be assumed to be an IFA by virtue of their population size alone,20 and that the distance between the proposed IFA and the location of the persecutors does not in itself serve to establish that the proposed IFA is viable.21

propositions.text: An IFA need not be far from the appellant's home if it is truly a refuge from persecution in their home district.
propositions.quote: That said, the IFA need not be far away from where the appellant has previously lived: the concept of an IFA does not require that the safe haven be in another city or province than the place of origin so long as it is truly an area in which the appellant can seek refuge from the persecution experienced in their home district.22

propositions.text: Whether the Appellants face a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA depends on their evidence and general principles.
propositions.quote: Ultimately, the question of whether an appellant has shown, on a balance of probabilities, that they face a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA will turn on their evidence, keeping in mind the general principles above. First Prong Proximity of the IFA

paragraphs.summary: Canadian courts hold urban areas aren't assumed IFAs by size; IFA need not be far; question depends on evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellants have a viable IFA in Kathmandu despite distance from their village.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that despite the distance between the Appellants' village and Kathmandu (XXXX XXXX according to the principal Appellant), they have a viable IFA in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: The Appellants submit they were only 80-90 km from Kathmandu during last Maoist encounter; Maoists have people everywhere.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that they were only 80-90 kilometres from Kathmandu when they had their last encounter with the Maoists. Additionally, the principal Appellant testified that the Maoists told them they have people in every part of the country.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Kathmandu a viable IFA; Appellants argue proximity and Maoists' nationwide presence negate this.

propositions.text: The RAD finds Appellants' statements about Maoists' ability to locate them anywhere are speculative and unsupported by objective evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD has discussed the Appellants' statements about the ability of the Maoists to locate them anywhere in the country previously and found it was grounded in speculation. The RAD has also confirmed the RPD finding that there is a lack of objective evidence supporting close ties, coordination, and communication between the Maoist faction in their home district and other Maoist groups throughout the country, including the capital city of Kathmandu.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants' claims of Maoists' nationwide reach speculative and unsupported by evidence.

propositions.text: The principal Appellant's statements show local Maoists stopped them for extortion, not to prevent fleeing, undermining evidence Maoists can locate them in IFA.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes that the principal Appellant confirmed in his statements in his BOC, as well as in his testimony, that in September 2015, at the time they were stopped in Mugline, they were still in their local district going about their regular process of delivering fruit to customers. The RAD finds that the statements indicate the local Maoist group did not stop them that day because they were attempting to flee the area, but because they were simply trying to extort more money from them. The RAD finds the Appellants' submissions are insufficient to support that this particular action provides persuasive evidence that the Maoists can locate them in the proposed IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds local Maoists stopped Appellants for extortion, not fleeing, so evidence Maoists can locate them in IFA is insufficient.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with the RPD finding on IFA proximity and rejects the Appellants' argument.
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the finding of the RPD in this issue and the Appellants' argument fails.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with the RPD and rejects the Appellants' argument on IFA proximity.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue Maoists are ruling party and state actors, so no IFA exists anywhere in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit the Maoists are currently the ruling party in Nepal, and that the agents of persecution in this case are, therefore, effectively state actors. The Appellants further argue that the Maoists hold power at the highest level of the Nepali government, and the government is ubiquitous in Nepal, therefore, it defies reason to suggest that the Appellants have an IFA anywhere in the country.

propositions.text: The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellants' argument that Maoists' ruling party status negates any IFA.
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Maoists' ruling party status negates any IFA; RAD is not persuaded.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows Maoists in Nepal are fragmented groups, some part of government, others opposed and violent.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the documentary evidence describes the Maoists in Nepal as a series of groups with various fragments or splinter offshoots. The documentary evidence states that "some of these groups are part of the government, while others are opposed to the government and are engaged in boycotts and violent activities."23 [citation omitted] The documentary evidence notes: "[t]here are a number of Maoist factions who have rejected accommodation with the elected government and continue political activity beyond the mainstream Maoist party," elements of which may be involved in extortion. [citation omitted] The evidence carries on to note: ...that instances of kidnapping and extortion by Maoist groups "are increasingly rare occurrences from a political party perspective" and are "not common any longer"... The same source indicated that "organized human rights violations/abuses are not taking place in Nepal due to the Maoist party," although there may be involvement in some criminal activities by "former, frustrated combatants in certain parts of Nepal." 24 [citation omitted]

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence shows Maoists are fragmented groups, some in government, others opposed and violent.

propositions.text: The RAD finds many splinter Maoist groups have broken from central Maoist identity; Appellants' problems were with Biplav faction.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that many of these splinter groups have broken away from the central "Maoist" identity and values. The RAD notes, as discussed previously, that all of the Appellants' problems with the Maoists occurred in their home area with a separatist Maoist faction (a splinter group) described as the Biplav faction (Netra Bikram Chand Biplav).25

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants' problems were with the Biplav splinter Maoist faction, not central Maoists.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence indicates Biplav faction is a dissident group involved in criminal activity and extortion, separate from peace process Maoists.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence indicates that this group, composed of former, frustrated combatants and other factions that have rejected accommodation with the elected government,26 is involved in criminal activity and extortion. The documentary evidence further confirms that the Unified Communist Party or Nepal-Maoists that joined the peace process in April 2006 has since split into five groups, one of which is the dissident Biplav's group.27

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence shows Biplav faction is dissident, involved in crime and extortion, separate from peace process Maoists.

propositions.text: In 2016, Biplav Maoists formed an independent local council defying government structures, mainly active outside Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The evidence notes that in 2016, the Biplav Maoists formed an independent local council in the XXXX area, stating that it would defy the structures of the present government and would implement the constitution made by the party.28 The RAD finds the documentary evidence indicates that the Biplav faction is a dissident group operating outside of the ruling government. They engage in extortion mainly outside of Kathmandu in the Mid-West and Far-West regions of Nepal.29 The RAD notes that the evidence demonstrates that these groups are considered violent, but it does not demonstrate that they have any influence or control over the current ruling government in Nepal.

paragraphs.summary: Biplav faction formed independent council in 2016, operates outside government, mainly outside Kathmandu, and is violent but lacks government control.

propositions.text: Evidence shows Maoist groups may be active in Kathmandu but not in extortion or kidnapping of individuals like the Appellants there.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes that while a few articles indicate the Maoist groups may be involved in activities in Kathmandu, the evidence does not indicate that they have been active in extortion and kidnapping of individuals with a profile similar to the Appellants in Kathmandu.

paragraphs.summary: Evidence shows Maoists may be active in Kathmandu but not in extortion or kidnapping of people like the Appellants there.

propositions.text: The agent of persecution is a dissident Maoist faction; little evidence links it to ruling groups in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the agent of persecution seeking the Appellants is a dissident faction of the larger grouping of organizations identified as "Maoists" in Nepal. The RAD has reviewed the Appellants' testimony and documentary evidence relating to these numerous groups in Nepal. The RAD notes the Appellants' evidence clearly identifies a local Maoist group of the Biplav faction as the agents of persecution. The RAD finds there is little persuasive evidence to allow it to find that the Biplav faction has any direct linkage to the ruling groups in Nepal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the persecutors are a dissident Maoist faction with little link to ruling groups.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Appellants' argument on this aspect must fail.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds this aspect of the Appellants' argument must fail.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD rejects this aspect of the Appellants' argument.

propositions.text: Whether the Appellants face risk relocating to Kathmandu due to being sought by local Biplav Maoist group.
propositions.quote: The RAD has considered if the Appellants will face risk in relocating to Kathmandu due to their profile as individuals who were being sought for extortion by their local Biplav Maoist group.

propositions.text: RPD found limited objective evidence that Maoists have nationwide network and weak interregional connections.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the objective evidence provides limited support to the Appellants' assertion that the Maoists have a nationwide network and operate throughout the country; further, it found little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the larger Maoist network.

propositions.text: Appellants argue evidence confirms Maoists have nationwide network able to find them anywhere in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the evidence confirms the Maoists have a nationwide network, giving them the ability to find them anywhere in Nepal.

propositions.text: Appellants submit RPD and documentary evidence confirm Maoists' nationwide network.
propositions.quote: The Appellants further submit that the RPD as well as the documentary evidence confirm this fact.

propositions.text: RAD is not persuaded by the Appellants' argument about Maoists' nationwide network.
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD considers risk from Maoists in Kathmandu; RPD found limited evidence of nationwide Maoist network; Appellants argue otherwise; RAD rejects their argument.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant's testimony about Maoists' network is speculative and lacks personal knowledge.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the Appellants' explanation provides little support for his allegations regarding the communication ability of the agent of persecution and that it is based on speculation.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant testified he was unclear how Maoists operate but believed they have large network to find them.
propositions.quote: He answered that he was not clear how they operate, but he knew that they have a large network to find them.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant heard about Maoists' network but had no personal knowledge of anyone harmed by them.
propositions.quote: He was asked to explain how he was aware of this information and testified that this was what he had heard, further stating that he had no personal knowledge of anyone who had experienced problems with the Maoists.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the principal Appellant's testimony about Maoists' network speculative and unsupported by personal knowledge.

propositions.text: Board's evidence states YCL has nationwide network but lacks detail on interregional communication or linkage to Biplav Maoists.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Board's objective evidence makes a statement that the Young Communist League (YCL), a youth offshoot of the Maoist party, has a "nationwide network," but beyond that, the detailed information in this document addressing the actions of the YCL towards those associated with opposing political views provides no additional information about the ability of various divisions to communicate and share information throughout the country.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence does not confirm linkage between YCL and Biplav Maoists or their communication/cooperation.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes that the documentary evidence does not confirm any linkage between the YCL and the Biplav Maoists. Nor does it make any mention of the ability of the numerous Maoist factions to communicate with each other or whether they would have any interest in sharing information due to their opposing political viewpoints.

propositions.text: Little evidence shows strength of connections or coordination among Maoist groups relevant to Appellants' case.
propositions.quote: The RAD's review of the documentary evidence finds little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the large number of Maoist groups, and if/how the different regions coordinate and share information, including in circumstances such as the Appellants.'

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds documentary evidence shows YCL's nationwide network but no proof of linkage or coordination with Biplav Maoists relevant to Appellants.

propositions.text: Nepal's communication infrastructure was largely destroyed in 2015 earthquake; telephone and mobile networks are poor to fair; internet penetration low.
propositions.quote: The RAD additionally notes that much of Nepal's communication infrastructure was destroyed in the 2015 earthquake. The country's telephone communication system is described as "poor," its mobile- cellular network is described as "fair," and internet penetration is 17.6 percent of the population.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence confirms communication is limited in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the documentary evidence confirms that communication is limited.

propositions.text: Statements about Maoist network are vague, non-specific, and unsupported by additional evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the singular statement in the documentary evidence, as well as the Appellants' statements about the Maoist "network," are vague and non-specific, and they are not supported by any additional evidence before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes Nepal's poor communication infrastructure and finds statements about Maoist network vague and unsupported.

propositions.text: Insufficient persuasive evidence supports Appellants' claim that Biplav Maoists can communicate nationwide to locate them.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds on its review of all of the evidence, that there is insufficient persuasive evidence to support the Appellant's allegations that the Biplav Maoists have an ability to communicate throughout Nepal in order to locate the Appellant.

propositions.text: RAD supports RPD's findings on this issue and rejects Appellants' argument.
propositions.quote: The RAD supports the findings of the RPD in this issue and the Appellants' argument must fail.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds insufficient evidence that Biplav Maoists can locate Appellants nationwide and supports RPD's findings, rejecting Appellants' argument.

propositions.text: RPD found local Maoists not seeking principal Appellant's brother or son in Kathmandu supports IFA viability.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the fact that the local Maoist group had not sought out the principal Appellant's brother or son living in Kathmandu during the past two years in an attempt to locate the Appellants, supported the viability of the IFA.

propositions.text: RPD found brother and son, both NCP supporters, reported no Maoist problems in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The RPD further found that the Appellants' testimony confirmed that the brother, who is an NCP supporter like the Appellants, and their son, the child of an NCP supporter, have not reported any problems with Maoists in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Appellants submit new evidence refutes RPD's finding about brother and son not targeted.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the new evidence submitted in support of their appeal refutes the RPD finding.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found local Maoists not targeting Appellants' brother or son supports IFA; Appellants submit new evidence refutes this.

propositions.text: RAD found new evidence submitted by Appellants not credible and did not admit it on appeal.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the new evidence relied on by the Appellants was assessed earlier in this decision and it was found not to be credible. The RAD did not admit this evidence in this appeal.

propositions.text: Appellants' arguments based on new evidence fail to show RPD erred.
propositions.quote: As such, the Appellants' arguments arising from the letter are unable to demonstrate that the RPD erred.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants' new evidence not credible and rejects their arguments that RPD erred.

propositions.text: Appellants did not contest RPD's finding that brother and son had no Maoist problems in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes the Appellants have not contested the RPD's finding in respect to the brother or the Appellants' son experiencing no problems from any Maoist factions in Kathmandu because of their association with the NCP.

propositions.text: RAD supports RPD findings and rejects Appellants' argument that Maoists sought brother and son to locate Appellants.
propositions.quote: The RAD supports the RPD findings in this issue and finds the Appellants' argument that they have provided persuasive evidence that the local Maoist group has sought out the principal Appellant's brother and son living in Kathmandu in an attempt to locate the Appellants, and that this impacts the RPD's IFA finding, must fail.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes Appellants did not contest RPD's finding about brother and son and rejects their argument that Maoists sought them.

propositions.text: To target Appellants in Kathmandu, Maoists must learn of their return, relocation to Kathmandu, and exact whereabouts.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that in order to target the Appellants in Kathmandu, the Biplav Maoists from the Appellants' home area would be required to: 1) Learn the Appellants have returned to Nepal; 2) Learn the Appellants have relocated to Kathmandu; and, 3) Determine the whereabouts of the Appellants in the city.

propositions.text: If Maoists had resources to track Appellants' presence, objective evidence would support this.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that if an individual or group had sufficient resources to be able to learn of a person's return to Nepal, and their presence in any area in Nepal, there would be objective evidence to support this.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Maoists would need to learn of Appellants' return, relocation, and location in Kathmandu, and such capacity would have objective evidence.

propositions.text: Insufficient credible evidence shows Maoists can track Appellants' arrival or movements in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds there is not enough sufficient credible evidence to establish that the agent of persecution has the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellants' return to Nepal upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellants' movements within Nepal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no credible evidence that Maoists can track Appellants' arrival or movements in Nepal.

propositions.text: On balance, no serious possibility Maoists in Kathmandu will target Appellants for political opinions.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, as did the RPD, that there is no serious possibility that Maoists in Kathmandu will target the Appellants based on their real or perceived political opinions (i.e. as NCP members or supporters).

propositions.text: Appellants have not shown serious possibility Biplav Maoists can locate them in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: In addition, the RAD finds that the Appellants have not advanced sufficient persuasive evidence that there is a serious possibility that the Biplav Maoists from their local area have the ability to locate the Appellants in Kathmandu.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no serious possibility Maoists will target Appellants in Kathmandu and Appellants failed to show Maoists can locate them there.

propositions.text: RPD found it objectively reasonable for Appellants to reside in Kathmandu given their circumstances.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that when it considered the Appellants' particular circumstances, it was objectively reasonable for them to reside in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant stated family could survive if Maoists not targeting them.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant stated that the family would be able to survive if the Maoists were not targeting them.

propositions.text: Appellants did not provide additional testimony or reasons why they could not reside in IFA location.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellants did not advance any additional testimony or provide reasons in their Memorandum as to why they would not be able to reside in the proposed IFA location.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant has 12 years education including some university.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant has twelve years of education, which includes some university education.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant has extensive work experience in two professions.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant has extensive work experience as both a XXXX and a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Associate Appellant worked as a XXXX person in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The associate Appellant has worked as a XXXX person in Nepal.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant has a brother in Kathmandu likely available to assist.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant has a brother in Kathmandu who would likely be available to assist the Appellants in their relocation.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant testified no barriers to finding employment or housing in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant testified that they did not face any barriers to finding employment or housing in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Appellants previously relocated within Nepal and are experienced international travellers.
propositions.quote: The Appellants provided testimony to indicate that they had relocated in Nepal on a previous occasion. The Appellants are experienced international travellers.

propositions.text: Appellants travelled to Canada and resettled without significant problems.
propositions.quote: They have travelled to Canada and resettled without reporting any significant problems.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found it reasonable for Appellants to reside in Kathmandu; RAD notes Appellants' education, work, family support, and travel experience.

propositions.text: Given Appellants' circumstances, relocating to Kathmandu is not unduly harsh or objectively unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds after a review of all of the evidence, that given the Appellants' personal circumstances, it is not unduly harsh or objectively unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Kathmandu in Nepal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concludes relocating to Kathmandu is not unduly harsh or unreasonable for Appellants.

propositions.text: RAD agrees with RPD that Kathmandu is a viable IFA; claim fails on this basis.
propositions.quote: Upon review of the appeal record, including the testimony of the Appellants, their documentary evidence and the information available in the NDP, the RAD agrees with the conclusion of the RPD for the same reasons, that Kathmandu offers the Appellants a viable IFA within Nepal; the claim therefore fails on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with RPD that Kathmandu is a viable IFA and dismisses the claim on that basis.

propositions.text: Once IFA named, burden is on Appellants to show either prong of Rasaratnam test not met.
propositions.quote: Once the IFA has been named, the burden is on the Appellants to show that either of the two prongs of the Rasaratnam test are not met.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that Biplav Maoists have reach or influence to locate Appellants in Nepal including Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: There is insufficient evidence in the record to suggest that the Biplav Maoists from their home region would have the reach or influence to locate the Appellants elsewhere in Nepal, including specifically in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Biplav Maoists cannot enlist other factions to conduct national search causing serious persecution risk.
propositions.quote: The RAD further finds that they would not be able to enlist other Maoist factions to conduct a national search for the Appellants, such that it would give rise to a serious possibility of persecution or subject them personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture.

propositions.text: Appellants have not shown proposed IFA would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh in their circumstances.
propositions.quote: Likewise, they have not demonstrated that in their personal circumstances, the proposed IFA would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh.

propositions.text: Burden rests with Appellants to show no IFA once raised; they have not discharged it here.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the burden of proof rests with the Appellant to show that they do not have an IFA to Kathmandu once raised, and the RAD finds that the Appellants have not discharged that burden.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD states burden on Appellants to disprove IFA; finds insufficient evidence Maoists can locate them or that IFA is unreasonable; burden not met.

propositions.text: RAD dismisses appeal and confirms RPD decision that Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms RPD decision that Appellants are not refugees or in need of protection under IRPA.
